newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: NATO ROW SET TO DOMINATE EUROPEAN SECURITY SUMMIT.
newsitem.headline: NATO ROW SET TO DOMINATE EUROPEAN SECURITY SUMMIT.

text.p: Leaders from Europe and North America begin a two-day European security summit on Monday to map out a future blueprint for peace but Russia's concerns over NATO expansion threaten to dominate the meeting.

Heads of state and government from the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) are expected to agree a final document that will lay out plans for European security in the 21st century, launch a new round of arms control talks and shore up peace in Bosnia.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, standing in for President Boris Yeltsin who is recovering from heart surgery, wasted no time in underscoring Moscow's opposition to NATO plans to take in former members of the now-defunct Warsaw Pact.

Speaking on the eve of the summit, Chernomyrdin repeated the tough line adopted by Russian leaders last week against the Western alliance's eastward expansion, which Moscow says would threaten Russia's security.
"Russia is categorically against NATO expanding eastwards," he told reporters after meeting Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres. "There is no need to rush."
"The fact that Europe is now without blocs is very important. We must work together. We must develop this, strengthen this," he added.
Western diplomats say they would prefer the Lisbon summit, which brings together the United States and Canada with European states, to avoid the debate on NATO enlargement.
The last OSCE summit two years ago in Budapest was wrecked by a row over the same issue and by differences over Bosnia.
The summit will be opened by Guterres at 9 a.m. (0900 GMT) with Chernomyrdin delivering the first delegation address 45 minutes later.

The leaders will also hold a series of bilateral meetings on the fringes of the summit. Chernomyrdin is scheduled to meet U.S. Vice President Al Gore, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac.

Representatives from Algeria, Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia, Japan and South Korea are also attending the summit. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived on Sunday night surrounded by police and security officials at his hotel in Estoril outside Lisbon.
Russia has little chance of winning support at the summit for its proposals to give the OSCE a more powerful role in European security and act as a counterbalance to NATO.
But by taking a hard line on NATO enlargement, Moscow may win concessions in talks on other issues at the summit, including adapting a 1990 treaty on conventional arms control.

The United States, represented by Gore who arrives on Monday morning, and most NATO states have indicated they will accept new talks next year on adapting and modernising the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty.

The pact, which commits 30 of the 54 OSCE states to cut military hardware such as tanks, aircraft and artillery, was concluded during the Cold War East-West divide. Moscow says that with the breakup of the Soviet Union, NATO forces are superior and a new balance must be worked out.
Officials worked into the night to reach final agreement on the summit documents on issues ranging from ethnic conflicts, human rights, freedom of the media and economic support.

One year after the end of the war in Bosnia, the meeting will agree a continued role for the OSCE there through 1997, working in parallel with the NATO-led peace force, with scope for a further extension through 1998.
Despite concerns over a possible NATO row, OSCE sources said they were more worried over positions being taken by Azerbaijan and Armenia which could scupper agreement on a final document.
Azerbaijan wants the summit to affirm its territorial integrity but Armenia opposes this because it wants the enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh to be given self-determination.

The last OSCE summit agreed to send a peacekeeping force to Nagorno-Karabakh, where Azerbaijanis and ethnic Armenians have fought to a stalemate, leaving the Armenians in control. Peace talks between Azerbaijan and Armenia have made little progress.
"If Azerbaijan and Armenia carry on as they are, we may have no final document at all," one OSCE source said. REUTER
